name: southern style cornbread
instructions:
From Daniel Gritzer, Serious Eats — 'Southern-Style Unsweetened Cornbread' — scaled DOWN to 1 EGG (× 1/3 of Gritzer's original). A small-batch, cornmeal-forward, minimally-sweet cornbread in a cast-iron skillet. Small batch is the right size for this recipe because it DOESN'T STORE WELL (see notes) — make less, eat fresh.

SERVES 3-4. Small cast-iron skillet (6-inch or small 8-inch), or a small loaf pan.

TWO VARIANTS:
- VARIANT A — GRITZER'S BUTTERMILK 1-EGG (TANGY) — the current front-runner. Buttermilk-based, tangy in the right way. Use this by default.
- VARIANT B — YOGURT-BASED 1-EGG (WORK IN PROGRESS) — yogurt substituted for buttermilk; needs balancing (more butter or added milk) to counter the extra tang. Not yet locked in.

=== VARIANT A — GRITZER'S BUTTERMILK 1-EGG (TANGY) ===

INGREDIENTS:
- 5 oz (1 cup) STONE-GROUND CORNMEAL (see CORNMEAL QUALITY note)
- 2/3 tsp kosher salt (Gritzer's salt runs high; 1/2 tsp is also fine)
- 2/3 tsp baking powder
- 1/4 tsp baking soda
- 1 tsp sugar (see SUGAR note — not optional)
- 5/6 cup buttermilk (~scant 1 cup — 3/4 cup + 2 tbsp)
- 1 large egg
- 4 tbsp (1/2 stick) UNSALTED BUTTER, melted, divided (or lard / bacon fat)

PROCEDURE:
1. Place the empty cast-iron skillet on the center rack of the oven and preheat to 375°F (190°C). The skillet PREHEATS WITH THE OVEN — this is what produces the crisp edges (see PREHEAT SKILLET note).
2. Meanwhile, whisk the cornmeal with salt, baking powder, baking soda, and sugar in a large bowl.
3. In a separate bowl, whisk the buttermilk with the egg until homogenous. Whisking constantly, drizzle in all but 1 tablespoon of the melted butter.
4. Whisk the wet into the dry JUST until thoroughly mixed. Avoid over-mixing.
5. Pour the remaining 1 tbsp melted butter into the preheated skillet and swirl to coat.
6. Scrape the batter into the hot skillet, smoothing gently. Bake until lightly browned on top and a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean — ~30-35 min.
7. Cool ~10-15 min in the skillet, then serve warm.

=== VARIANT B — YOGURT-BASED 1-EGG (WORK IN PROGRESS) ===

Using yogurt in place of buttermilk (common substitution when buttermilk isn't on hand) overshoots the tang — yogurt is more concentrated / tangier than buttermilk and a straight sub reads too sour. Adjusted ratios rebalance for less tang, more lift, more sweet buffer. Still WIP — the balancing knob (more butter vs added milk) hasn't been locked in yet.

INGREDIENTS:
- 5 oz (1 cup) STONE-GROUND CORNMEAL
- 1/2 tsp salt (down from Variant A's 2/3)
- 1 tsp baking powder (up from Variant A's 2/3 — needs more lift with the thicker liquid)
- 1/4 tsp baking soda (same)
- 1 tbsp sugar (up from Variant A's 1 tsp — more sugar buffers the yogurt tang)
- 3/4 cup yogurt (less liquid than Variant A's 5/6 cup buttermilk)
- 1 large egg
- 4-6 tbsp butter (start at 4; might need up to 6 to balance the yogurt tang)

PROCEDURE: same as Variant A.

BALANCING KNOB (STILL TO DECIDE):
- Option 1 — MORE BUTTER (bump from 4 to 6 tbsp) to add fat that softens the yogurt tang.
- Option 2 (WANT TO TRY) — SOME MILK IN THE LIQUID rather than more butter. Rough sketch: ~1/2 cup yogurt + ~1/4 cup milk = 3/4 cup total, with butter kept at 4 tbsp. Untested; this is the experimental direction to work on next time.

Doesn't keep well (either variant) — eat fresh (see notes).
notes:
Source: Daniel Gritzer, Serious Eats — 'Southern-Style Unsweetened Cornbread' (November 2015, updated February 2025). Written down at the 1-EGG (× 1/3) scale because it doesn't store well and small-batch is the right fit for this recipe.

=== SMALL-BATCH IS THE RIGHT SIZE — DOESN'T STORE WELL ===

Cornbread loses its texture as it cools past the day-of window. Eat while fresh. Day-old cornbread is still useful for dressing / stuffing applications (per Gritzer + the comments) but the standalone eating experience degrades.

Because the storage-life is short, making a smaller batch is almost always the right call — the 1-egg version here fits 3-4 servings, which is roughly what gets eaten same-day. Scaling up to 2 or 3 eggs (Gritzer's full recipe) is fine if you're feeding more people or want dressing leftovers, but for regular eating the 1-egg scale is optimal.

=== EARLIER EXPERIMENT — HANDROLLED VERSION WITH REDUCED BUTTERMILK (CLEARED) ===

Earlier iterations of this file documented a handrolled version that cut Gritzer's buttermilk (from 2.5 cups down to 1 cup for the full 3-egg scale) and reduced butter proportionally. That version came out EGGY and A BIT DRY — the reduced buttermilk and butter left the eggs proportionally dominant and the crumb under-hydrated.

Lesson: Gritzer's ~1:1 cornmeal-to-buttermilk ratio is what makes the crumb work. Ballard's Feast and Farm southern cornbread converges on the same ratio (2 cups cornmeal to 1 3/4 cups buttermilk). Two independent southern-cornbread references landing on the same wet ratio is a real signal that under-hydration is the wrong direction. Gritzer's version at proportional scale-down is the current recipe.

=== CORNMEAL QUALITY IS THE WHOLE DISH ===

Gritzer is emphatic: the cornmeal itself has the single biggest impact on the final cornbread. High-quality stone-ground cornmeal (a variety of textures from floury to coarse) is what produces a light, fluffy bread with crackly bits of corn grit and real corn flavor. Mass-market industrial cornmeal (uniform grind from underripe corn) doesn't work — reads flat and 'sub-zero on the sweetness scale.'

RECOMMENDED SOURCES (from Gritzer): Anson Mills, Old Mill of Guilford, Nora Mill. Order online or seek out a local mill.

=== SUGAR — 1 TSP AT 1-EGG SCALE, NOT OPTIONAL IN PRACTICE ===

Gritzer frames sugar as optional (only for mass-market cornmeal). In practice — even with good stone-ground cornmeal — a small amount is right. 1 tsp per 1 cup cornmeal (× 1/3 of Gritzer's 1 tbsp for 3 cups). Keep the sugar. The dish is still 'unsweetened' in the sense that it's not a sweet cornbread; the sugar just balances the flavor. Skipping makes the finished bread read incomplete.

=== NO WHEAT FLOUR — SOUTHERN STYLE, OPPOSITE OF NORTHERN ===

This is the Southern-style shape: cornmeal only, no wheat flour, no (or minimal) sugar. Northern-style cornbread uses wheat flour to correct for coarse industrial grind and sugar to compensate for less-ripe corn. Different dish. If you want a sweeter/cake-like cornbread, reach for [[sweet-potato-cornbread]] instead — that one is explicitly more of a cake.

=== PREHEAT THE CAST IRON SKILLET — CRISP EDGES ===

Put the empty cast iron skillet in the oven while it preheats. Pour the batter into the already-hot skillet. This is what produces the crisp edges the recipe is known for. Skip this step and you get a softer-edged bread that's fine but not the same dish.

=== FAT — BUTTER, OR LARD / BACON FAT ===

Melted butter is the default. LARD or BACON FAT also work well (per Gritzer) — push the register more traditional-southern. Same quantity (4 tbsp / 1/2 stick at 1-egg scale).

=== DOESN'T RISE MUCH ===

General observation: this cornbread doesn't rise much regardless of leavener quantity. Don't expect a tall fluffy loaf; expect a dense-ish flat-topped bake. That's what it is.

=== WANT TO TRY — CHEDDAR CHEESE + JALAPEÑO VARIANTS ===

Two variant directions worth testing on top of the base Gritzer recipe:

- CHEDDAR CHEESE folded into the batter (or scattered on top before baking). ~1/4 to 1/2 cup grated cheddar at 1-egg scale. Melting cheddar reads well with cornmeal + buttermilk — classic american cornbread move. Sharp cheddar for more character; mild for smoother integration.
- JALAPEÑOS diced and folded in. 1-2 jalapeños at 1-egg scale, seeds removed for milder heat or kept for real heat. Fresh (raw diced) or pickled both work.
- BOTH TOGETHER: the classic cheddar-and-jalapeño combo — pairs cleanly with the savory cornmeal base and pushes the dish more distinctly southwestern.

All untested at this scale. Standard southern-cornbread variations worth capturing as directions to explore.

=== SCALING UP (IF NEEDED) ===

For larger batches, scale everything × 2 or × 3 from the 1-egg version above:

| Ingredient | 1 egg (base) | 2 eggs | 3 eggs (Gritzer's original) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cornmeal | 1 cup / 5 oz | 2 cups / 10 oz | 3 cups / 15 oz |
| Buttermilk | ~5/6 cup | ~1 2/3 cups | 2 1/2 cups |
| Butter | 4 tbsp | 8 tbsp | 12 tbsp (1 1/2 sticks) |
| Salt | 2/3 tsp | 1 1/3 tsp | 2 tsp |
| Baking powder | 2/3 tsp | 1 1/3 tsp | 2 tsp |
| Baking soda | 1/4 tsp | 1/2 tsp | 3/4 tsp |
| Sugar | 1 tsp | 2 tsp | 1 tbsp |
| Eggs | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| Skillet | 6-inch or small 8-inch | 9-inch | 12-inch |
| Bake time | ~30-35 min | ~40 min | ~45 min |

At 375°F throughout.

=== SIBLING RECIPE — SWEET POTATO CORNBREAD ===

[[sweet-potato-cornbread]] (Anita Spring Councel, Southern Roots) is the sweeter, cake-like cornbread in this cookbook. Includes wheat flour, sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, orange zest, and mashed sweet potato. Different register entirely.

When to reach for which:
- SWEET POTATO CORNBREAD: sweet, cake-like, pairs with cream cheese frosting or savory ham/prosciutto.
- THIS RECIPE (SOUTHERN UNSWEETENED): cornmeal-forward, dense corn flavor, savory register, meant to go with beans/greens/chili or under a savory main.
